models.summary: A four-sector New Keynesian DSGE model, built on Barrdear and Kumhof (2016) and Qian (2018), judges whether a central bank can issue a digital currency. Qian assumes the new currency fully replaces cash, which the paper calls unrealistic, so the holding share is left free and three cases are run: full replacement, half, and none. Households face a real budget and a deposit-in-advance constraint, and a shock shifts them from deposits toward the digital currency. Two tiers of firms, Dixit-Stiglitz final goods and Cobb-Douglas intermediate goods, borrow all their capital and wages, and pay to change prices and capital. Banks fund themselves from deposits or central-bank loans and lend or hold reserves, inside an interest-rate corridor. The central bank balances its sheet and sets the rate by a Taylor-type rule aimed at inflation. Output equals consumption plus investment plus the two adjustment costs plus lending costs. Calibrated to a 3 percent benchmark rate, beta 0.971, capital share 0.7, the steady state under full replacement gives a reserve ratio of 17.8 percent and consumption at 75 percent of output, closest to the world's roughly 15 percent and 80 percent. A positive digital shock lifts consumption and output.

models.summary: Fourteen indicators for countries above 20 million people or 100 billion dollars of output, stratified into eight income bands, are reduced by principal components. Components are kept when the eigenvalue exceeds 1 and the running share passes 80 percent. Four survive, explaining 80.2 percent. The paper reads the first as access (inflation, corruption, credit rating), the second as growth (broad money, output, budget), the third as stability (population, unemployment) and the fourth as security (broad money over reserves, exchange rate). Each reading is backed by a story: inflation because digital currency was born to stop over-issue, savings because they carry people through a crisis.

models.summary: Twelve thematic areas of a financial system, from banks to digital currencies, are each scored on four axes taken from the UK HM Treasury risk assessment: vulnerability, likelihood, structural risk and risk after mitigation. Each area becomes a four-vector. Eleven areas train a k nearest neighbour classifier; digital currency is held out. With k equal to 3 and Euclidean distance, its three nearest neighbours all sit in the low class, matching the published label. The paper reads that as licence to copy the supervision used for casinos, high-value dealers and retail betting, and to rerun the grade each year to see the trend.

models.summary: A spatial autoregressive model on 163 countries tracks three economic freedom indices, financial, overall and trade, from the Heritage Foundation and the Wall Street Journal. Each index depends on its own lag and on a distance-weighted average of other countries, with distance measured between capitals. Tunisia, which made a digital currency official in 2015 and then saw its indices rise, is the test case: its three freedoms are lifted 10 percent and the model is re-solved. The indirect effect, Tunisia itself removed, is positive for most countries, so the paper claims a spillover onto banking efficiency, growth and trade openness. A rerun at 5 percent keeps the sign.
